entries.title: CrossFire's network
body: Smilegate's account of CrossFire begins with a problem. Its Korean service launched in 2007 into a market where other shooters already had established players. The studio needed more than a finished game to find an audience. Working with Tencent, it studied the Chinese market and reached players through QQ messenger. That connection matters: a multiplayer game needs people who can find one another and keep returning. The network around the software became part of the way this Korean-developed shooter reached its Chinese audience.

Smilegate dates the official Chinese service to 2008, separating it from the Korean beginning. Its retrospective also describes CrossFire Stars, the competition organised under its own name from 2013. An online shooter could become a recurring event as well as an application on a computer. Teams, tournaments and spectators gave repeated play a public setting. This account comes from the game's developer, celebrating its own success; the concrete history is the partnership and the infrastructure it built, rather than a claim that one title represents every Chinese player.

Tencent's 2022 results describe CrossFire as a game it had operated for fourteen years. The company singled out changes to player-versus-environment play and ranked competition as ways of sustaining the PC version. Those are decisions about what returning players do, not simply improvements to the image. A service has to give equipment and habits another purpose. The publisher's report makes that maintenance visible: work on modes and competitive structure sits alongside the more easily noticed work of launching a new game.

In 2015, Tencent published CrossFire Mobile, developed by TiMi Studio Group. Its 2022 report describes the mobile game as an expansion of the franchise's audience in China. This was a related product made for another device, rather than proof that the PC game had simply moved unchanged onto a phone. Looking at the two together reveals a particular route through games history: a Korean studio's shooter, a Chinese publishing and social network, continuing PC development, and a mobile team each contributed to the reach of one shared name.

entries.title: What sits behind a library
entries.summary: An account changes how a collection works.
body: Valve announced the Steam client's release on 12 September 2003. Twenty years later, its anniversary page arranged the service's history around each year's leading releases, mixing games with illustrations and memories of popular culture. That was one way to make an expanding service understandable: start with the titles people encountered there. Yet a library view tells only part of the story. Behind the remembered games are accounts, software and rules of access. Following those less visible parts shows how a collection can depend on a continuing relationship with a platform.

The Steam Subscriber Agreement describes access to software as a licence. In the version consulted in 2026, buying content does not transfer ownership of its intellectual property, and an account or subscription cannot simply be transferred except where Valve permits it. The everyday idea of a personal collection therefore sits inside a specific agreement. This distinction helps explain the design of a digital library, without treating today's contract as evidence of every rule in 2003. The relevant questions are which account has access and what that access includes.

Valve's developer documentation explains another connection between a game and its platform. The Steam DRM wrapper checks ownership and starts Steam before starting the game so that Steamworks features can function. It is a particular integration tool, not evidence that every title uses the same protection. For a developer, launching a game can involve services outside its own executable. For a player, those steps may appear as one ordinary click. The documentation makes that small sequence legible, showing some of the software relationships hidden behind the library's Play button.

Steam Families, released in 2024, made eligible games accessible across a family group while keeping personal saves and achievements. Multiple copies determined how many people could play the same title together. Developers could also exclude games, and technical requirements could limit sharing. These details show why a shared library is more than a row of borrowed covers. It has to organise separate people, available copies and progress. The result offers a particular kind of household access, shaped by software and participation rules rather than by passing a physical disc between hands.

entries.title: The work between adventures
entries.summary: EVE players organise help as well as conflict.
body: EVE Online's corporations can bring together people with different jobs, schedules and priorities. In 2023, CCP described managing these organisations as demanding work and presented Corporation Projects as a way to make contributions clearer. A shared goal could specify what the group needed and recognise members who helped. The interesting activity was not confined to flying a ship. Deciding what should happen, explaining it to other people and recording their efforts could shape the experience of belonging to the corporation as much as a battle did.

For the Havoc expansion, CCP announced automatic payments for completed project contributions, a way to copy recurring projects, and a manager role that let leaders delegate the task. New contribution types included scanning signatures and manufacturing items. These tools put routine coordination inside the game: a group could explain what it needed and recognise work that was easy to overlook. The announcement is useful because it names the administrative problem. Supporting a community meant reducing the effort required to keep track of people, materials and shared plans.

Other players organised around assistance rather than a corporation's production targets. In March 2024, Katia Sae reported that EvE-Scout's rescue division had helped its five-thousandth stranded pilot. The participant account describes both search-and-rescue operations and supply caches placed in wormhole space. The figure is the organisation's own reported milestone, but the practical arrangement is clear. Someone who cannot find a route home can depend on preparations made by people they may never have met. Exploration creates a reason for volunteers to maintain a public service.

CCP's January 2025 community report recognised EvE-Scout's approaching tenth anniversary. Alongside rescues, it described a website tracking connections through Thera and Turnur and a public folder of bookmarks. Sharing navigational knowledge could shorten another pilot's journey. The publisher's celebratory account is one perspective on the group, not an independent assessment of every player relationship. It nevertheless documents a useful form of community work: keeping information available, updating routes and making another person's passage possible. In this part of EVE, a lasting contribution can be a path someone else follows.

entries.title: Connected distribution
body: In July 2008, Apple described an App Store delivering software to an iPhone or iPod touch. A game could arrive through the device's wireless connection, with purchases charged to an iTunes account. By 14 July, Apple reported more than 800 applications and over ten million downloads across all categories. Those figures describe the company's first-weekend announcement, including software other than games. For mobile play, finding software, paying for it and beginning to use it could happen through one connected device.

Apple's launch report emphasised applications using Multi-Touch, an accelerometer and hardware-accelerated graphics. A phone had its own inputs alongside the familiar button arrangements of consoles. Its sensors and screen gave developers different materials to work with. Distribution continued after the first download: the store notified users when updates were available. The platform linked the way someone obtained a game with the way software could change. These were possibilities described at launch; individual games could choose which of the device's available features to use.

Apple's March 2019 Arcade announcement addressed a different difficulty. The company said paid games could struggle to reach audiences when competing with free titles, and proposed one subscription to a curated collection. It also described contributing to development costs. This was an announcement of a service planned for later that year, not evidence that its promised catalogue was already available in March. The change concerned the relationship between player, maker and shop: trying another game would no longer require another individual purchase within the collection Apple described.

The announced Arcade collection promised complete games without advertising or additional purchases, offline play, and continuity across supported Apple devices. Those conditions described an environment for choosing and continuing a game. They also differed from the free and individually priced titles on the store. The history is an adjustment of the platform's offer over time. The company that made individual downloads convenient proposed another way to browse and fund games, placing curation and a subscription alongside the store it operated, rather than replacing its earlier approaches.

entries.title: An audience gets involved
entries.summary: Watching can become another way of participating.
body: In February 2014, Twitch staff described a peculiar broadcast: chat messages controlled a single Pokémon game. Viewers were no longer only watching someone else's choices. Their own commands entered the same sequence, sometimes helping progress and sometimes working against one another. Twitch's contemporary account also noted fan art, a subreddit and a shared progress document. The activity already extended beyond the game window. People made ways to follow what the crowd was doing, turning an awkward shared controller into a subject that could be watched, discussed and recorded together.

On 1 March, Twitch reported that the group had finished after more than sixteen days. Its account mixed completion statistics with the nicknames, rivalries and jokes that viewers had built around the run. Anarchy and Democracy had become part of the shared vocabulary. This was Twitch celebrating its own community, but the document preserves a concrete change in the audience's role. A familiar adventure acquired another layer of meaning through the difficulty of controlling it collectively. Watching the struggle and explaining it to others became activities alongside entering commands.

Games Done Quick offers a different relationship between players and spectators. Its charity marathons present high-level speedrunning to an audience, bringing runners together with commentators, hosts and volunteers. The performance depends on a skilled person playing and people who explain and organise what viewers see. The organisation recognises that work when thanking those contributors. A broadcast can make a demanding route through a game understandable to someone who does not know it, placing that demonstration inside a fundraising event with a shared audience.

GDQ's community programmes show that a stream is a place to find other participants. Frame Fatales welcomes women and femmes interested in speedrunning; Black in a Flash supports Black runners; Games Done Queer highlights LGBTQIA+ participants. Hotfix offers community showcases beyond the main marathons. These are the organisation's stated purposes on its current site. They reveal another part of producing play for an audience: deciding who gets a stage and maintaining spaces where people can take part, learn from one another and appear before viewers.

entries.title: Who makes games
body: On 10 July 2023, CWA announced that SEGA of America workers had voted 91–26 to form a union. The bargaining unit crossed departments, bringing localisation, quality assurance, product development, sales and marketing into one organisation. Its members worked in Irvine and Burbank, California. Jobs usually separated in a production chart now shared a representative body. A finished game depended on more than its visible creative roles; the people helping it reach players could organise around their shared workplace and responsibilities.

Translator Ángel Gómez described the election as a chance to protect valued work while improving pay, benefits and stability. The announcement also named balanced workloads, flexibility and opportunities to advance as bargaining goals. Those were demands at the beginning of a process, not terms already secured by winning a vote. The distinction gives the story its next step: people from different departments had formed an organisation, but still had to negotiate what its presence would change in their working lives.

In March 2024, Communications Workers of America announced ratification of a first contract for its SEGA of America bargaining unit. The union described roles spanning translation, production, marketing and quality assurance. Among the provisions it reported was a commitment to credit workers, including early QA testers. This was one negotiated agreement, covering a specific group of employees rather than everyone under the SEGA name. It connected a public record on screen with the conditions under which different people contributed to a game's production.

The announcement described pay rises, protection against arbitrary discipline, layoff provisions and a labour-management committee. Those terms concerned the workplace as well as any finished game. A credit can preserve a contribution without settling the conditions in which the next contribution is made. For this particular bargaining unit in California, credit became one term within a larger arrangement about employment. The union's account describes recognition alongside compensation and protections, putting the conditions of production back inside the history of games for the people performing that work.

entries.title: Shared spaces
body: In April 2020, Getty introduced an Animal Crossing art generator. It connected open-content collection images to custom patterns that players could bring into New Horizons. A painting could become a shirt, flag or object in a player-made gallery. The project joined a museum collection to tools people used to arrange their islands. It answered a question: how could someone encounter and rearrange museum art while spending time inside a game instead of visiting a building? The player's arrangement gave the collection another setting.

Getty built on the open-source Animal Crossing Pattern Tool and added collection searching and a converter for IIIF image records. Open-access material from other museums could enter the same process. Several kinds of work met here: collection images, a community-made tool and a museum team adapting the interface. Getty described the project as independent of Nintendo. An institution could contribute to a shared activity without having designed the game, using a tool to bring its collection into places that players were making.

After its March 2020 closure, Monterey Bay Aquarium used game streams to reconnect with audiences. Staff Dana Allen-Greil and Emily Simpson later described how New Horizons' fish and other creatures offered openings for live interpretation. Catching an ocean sunfish led to an extended conversation with viewers about the animal. The game provided a shared object of attention; staff expertise and audience questions carried the discussion further. This is a documented institutional experiment, not evidence that a virtual island replaced the aquarium or that every player experienced the pandemic in the same way.

The National Videogame Museum's Animal Crossing Diaries call invited players to submit their experiences during COVID-19. It named both everyday routines and elaborate celebrations, and proposed combining contributions with interviews and articles. That collecting choice widened what could count as games history. A game was not only its release, rules or sales: it also held occasions that people wanted to remember. The invitation leaves room for different experiences rather than declaring a single story about lockdown. Preserving those accounts makes the people around the software part of the historical record.

entries.title: Keep the evidence
body: The Video Game History Foundation's digital library opened in 2025 with development papers, magazines, press materials and production footage. Phil Salvador highlighted producer Mark Flitman's paperwork and backups, alongside material from Cyan's Myst productions. These records let researchers ask questions that playing a game cannot answer alone. How was it presented to a publisher? What did a production need to organise? A plan or recording can place a familiar image among the decisions and practical work that brought it into existence, with people and circumstances attached.

Cataloguing and text recognition made the materials searchable. The library's launch FAQ distinguished processed, digitised holdings from material awaiting work, and explained that access did not automatically grant reproduction rights. These details are part of preservation. Someone needs to identify an object, describe its origin and explain what a researcher can do with it. The collection remains a developing body of evidence. A search result opens a route into that work, while collection descriptions help visitors understand the scope and limits of what they find.

Jordan Mechner's 2012 recovery of Prince of Persia's Apple II source code makes those dependencies tangible. The disks survived, but reading them required specialist help. Jason Scott and Tony Diaz worked on the recovery, while disk programmer Roland Gustafsson explained disk routines that made the files difficult to interpret. The evidence depended on equipment, technical knowledge and people who remembered their work. Recovering the data connected a physical object to knowledge the object could not explain by itself, bringing old production decisions into contact with new expertise.

Mechner explained why source code mattered even though people could play the game. It let someone interested in making or studying software examine the underlying work. His repository notice distinguishes studying the code from obtaining rights to the continuing franchise. A particular document becomes available, with its context and limitations. Alongside catalogued production papers, that recovery suggests a museum practice: identify what survives, preserve the information around it and let visitors follow evidence behind a familiar title. Availability begins an investigation rather than completing the history.
